rationale: Both note that exceptions exist for gifts/low-value goods and that the strict EU-wide customs rule only dates to July 2021, not a decade or more.
Both correct the author's name to Max Ghenis and cite the same ~515x marginal GiveWell figure instead of 1,500x.
Both make the identical core point that the 45% is Zvi Mowshowitz's own subjective estimate, not Sol's self-assessment.

Although both conclude Herbst didn't rely exclusively on AI Overviews, the old note grounds this in specific cited studies (Tow Center/CJR, BBC/EBU) while the new note cites entirely different substantiating facts (WIRED's own fact-checking process, personal chatbot tests, training-data vs. archives) with no overlap in supporting evidence.
Both state the game is not out of print due to a Gamefound-funded second printing that is nearly fulfilled and sold via similar retailers.
Both notes agree June 26 was only a partial easing of controls on Mythos while Fable remained restricted, with full elimination on both occurring June 30.
Both notes establish the 67% figure is PC-specific (not overall/global) and from an earlier report, undermining the claim.
Both identify the same source (Stat Significant, karaoke playlists from Spotify/Apple Music) and the same debunked claim (not Chartmetric).
Both notes clarify Sol/Terra/Luna are independent capability tiers, not subagents, and that 'ultra mode' is Sol's real subagent feature.
Both notes trace the 30% figure to a Texas university study (not UC Berkeley) and note Berkeley's actual A rates stayed stable at 30-35%.
Both notes reverse the claim, showing the paper itself (not just the blog post) explicitly addresses phenomenal consciousness while limiting itself to functional access consciousness.
Both notes state the research found AI agents are far more (not similarly) responsive to nudges than humans.
Both identify the figures as pre-correction and give the same corrected values (~205,000 / ~420,000 QALYs).
Both give the same Phoenix release date (Jan 20, 2026) and state no confirmed changes occurred between April and June.
Both make the same point that Opus 4.8 and Fable are Anthropic models, not OpenAI GPT models.
Both confirm the $2/$6 base price but reject the $4/$18 fast tier, citing the same $4/$12 priority-tier correction.
Both rebut the 'substantially behind on cyber' claim using the same Semgrep and Graphistry benchmark evidence showing GLM-5.2 matching/beating Opus.
Both correct the growth figure to ~200% YoY revenue growth rather than ~60%, with the same underlying report citation.
Both conclude the 572 figure misrepresents the Intelligence Index's actual model count, which is roughly 145-165 rather than 572.
Both correct the same date range error, stating Graetz & Michaels (2018) covered 1993-2007, not 1980-2000.
